cards.explanation: The answer is the house of the LORD in Jerusalem. Hezekiah, king of Judah, sends word and letters inviting everyone to come there (2 Chronicles 30:1). One address, no confusion. I wish my own directions were that clear, friends. "Follow the smell of cookies" only gets you so far.

The answer is to keep it in the second month. The king, his officials and the whole assembly in Jerusalem decide that (2 Chronicles 30:2). They missed the regular time, so they pick a new one. I think that's the right kind of stubborn, friends. They don't skip it, they just reschedule it, and I've rescheduled plenty of batches myself. The cookies still came out fine.

The answer is that too few priests were consecrated and the people weren't gathered. The text says not enough priests had consecrated themselves, and the people hadn't been gathered in Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 30:3). Two things weren't ready, so the regular time passed. Think of a bakery trying to open with half the staff still tying aprons, friends. The doors just can't open yet.

The answer is True. The text says, “This plan pleased the king and the whole assembly.” (2 Chronicles 30:4) Everybody's on board, from the king down. That's rare, friends. I can't even get a room to agree on which cookie shape goes first.

The answer is True. The letter says, “Children of Israel, return to the LORD, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, so that He may return to those of you who remain…” (2 Chronicles 30:6). It's an invitation to come back, with a promise attached. Most mail I get is a bill, friends, so I'd read this one twice.

The answer is sanctuary. The letter says, “Submit to the LORD and come to His sanctuary, which He has consecrated forever.” (2 Chronicles 30:8) Instead of stiff necks, the people are called to bow low and come to the place God set apart. Stiff necks and baking don't mix, friends. Ask my mustache about the first week I tried to bend over a rolling pin.

The answer is False. The letter holds out hope. It says, “For if you return to the LORD, your brothers and sons will receive mercy in the presence of their captors and will return to this land.” (2 Chronicles 30:9) Mercy for the captured ones and a way home. That's a good reason to turn around, friends.

The answer is that He is gracious and merciful. The letter gives the reason itself: “For the LORD your God is gracious and merciful…” (2 Chronicles 30:9). They can count on Him because of who He is. Nothing else needs to be on the list, friends.

The answer is that they scorn and mock them. The couriers travel from city to city through Ephraim and Manasseh as far as Zebulun, “…but the people scorned and mocked them.” (2 Chronicles 30:10) A king's invitation, and that's the reply. I think that one stings, friends.

The answer is True. The text says, “Nevertheless, some from Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun humbled themselves and came to Jerusalem.” (2 Chronicles 30:11) The mockers didn't get the last word. Some people heard that invitation and came, and I love that for them, friends.

The answer is one heart to obey the king's command. The text says the power of God was on the people in Judah “…to give them one heart to obey the command of the king and his officials according to the word of the LORD.” (2 Chronicles 30:12) One heart, and it comes with the power of God. I've watched six cookie cutters argue over one counter, friends, so I know that's no small gift.

The answer is the altars and the incense altars. The text says they proceeded to remove the altars in Jerusalem and take away the incense altars (2 Chronicles 30:14). They're clearing the city before the Passover. I clean my bakery before guests arrive too, friends. The difference is I only sweep up crumbs.

The answer is that they throw them into the Kidron Valley. The text says they took away the incense altars and threw them into the Kidron Valley (2 Chronicles 30:14). That's a full clear-out, friends. They didn't just push them to the side. I once swept a whole batch of burnt crumbs behind the oven, and this crowd would not approve.

The answer is ashamed. The text says, “The priests and Levites were ashamed, and they consecrated themselves…” (2 Chronicles 30:15). Then they got moving and did something about it. I think it takes a humble heart to stand there and say, okay, let's fix this. That's good baking and good living, friends.

The answer is False. The text says these people did not sit out. Many from Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar and Zebulun had not purified themselves, “…yet they ate the Passover, contrary to what was written.” (2 Chronicles 30:18) They came to the table without being cleansed first. That's why the next verse matters so much, friends.

The answer is that he speaks up for them before the LORD. The text says Hezekiah interceded for them (2 Chronicles 30:18). He stood in the gap and prayed. I think a king who prays for the crowd instead of scolding them is worth following, friends.

The answer is the one who sets his heart on seeking God. Hezekiah prays for “…everyone who sets his heart on seeking God…” (2 Chronicles 30:18-19). The heart is what he lifts up in the prayer. Seeking God is the thing he names, and I think that's a very good thing to be known for, friends.

The answer is True. The text says, “And the LORD heard Hezekiah and healed the people.” (2 Chronicles 30:20) Hezekiah prayed, and the LORD answered. I love how short that verse is, friends. It doesn't need a speech.

The answer is that he encourages them. The text says Hezekiah encouraged all the Levites who performed skillfully before the LORD (2 Chronicles 30:22). A king noticing good work and saying so. I'd cry happy tears if somebody did that after my first pan of cookies, friends.

The answer is to keep the feast seven more days. The text says, “The whole assembly agreed to observe seven more days…” (2 Chronicles 30:23). Seven days of joy, then seven more. I've seen a party fade the minute the cookies run out, friends. They kept this one going for seven more days.

The answer is False. The text names a wide crowd. The whole assembly of Judah rejoiced along with the priests, the Levites, the assembly from Israel, and the foreigners who came from Israel and those who lived in Judah (2 Chronicles 30:25). Everybody's invited into the joy, friends. I'd want a crowd like that in my bakery.

The answer is Solomon. The text says nothing like this had happened in Jerusalem since the days of Solomon, David's son and king of Israel (2 Chronicles 30:26). That's a big comparison, friends. The verse points all the way back to Solomon's days.

The answer is that it reaches God's holy dwelling in heaven. The text says the priests and Levites stood to bless the people, and God heard their voice, “…and their prayer came into His holy dwelling place in heaven.” (2 Chronicles 30:27) They blessed, God heard, and the prayer came into heaven. That's the whole answer, friends, and it's worth a quiet moment.
